extracted.intended_audience: authors of scientific papers and technical documents preparing figures and charts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for designing, producing, and integrating figures/plots/diagrams into scientific or technical papers, including workflow, time planning, consistency with typography, labeling, and avoiding misleading or distracting visual elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply guidelines only when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow general guidelines blindly — guidelines are usually created for specific situations and may not fit yours. The basic rule: 'Every rule can be broken, as long as you are aware that you are breaking a rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying or breaking a guideline ask: (1) Does this guideline really address my situation? (2) If I do the opposite, will the advantages outweigh the disadvantages the guideline was supposed to prevent? Be conscious when you break a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan time for creating graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a graphic needs as much time to create as a text of the same length; treat graphics as first-class citizens of your paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate roughly one hour per page for a text first draft (author's example); a half-page graphic might take ~0.5 hour for first draft and 1–2 hours for revisions later. Difficult/high-information-density graphics may require more time; do not treat graphics as an afterthought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic creation workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow an iterative authoring process for graphics analogous to writing: decide message, outline, draft, revise repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) Decide what the graphic should communicate (explicitly state the intended message). (2) Create a rough outline/shape (pencil & paper useful). (3) Fill in finer details to create a first draft. (4) Revise the graphic repeatedly along with the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make standalone figures understandable by themselves (captions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-alone figures will often be viewed apart from the text that refers to them, so captions must provide sufficient context to make the figure self-contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A caption should identify what is shown, refer to the location of the relevant text (e.g., 'introduced on page xyz'), and add contextual explanatory detail. Don't fear multi-line (even ~5-line) captions if needed. Reference figures from the main text (e.g., 'For an example... see Figure 2.1 on page xyz').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference figures with full word 'Figure' (avoid abbreviations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer writing out 'Figure 2.1' instead of 'Fig. 2.1' so the reader doesn't misinterpret sentence-ending punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes editorial disagreement about this, but recommends avoiding abbreviations; weigh space savings vs clarity and editorial constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not scale graphics arbitrarily
rubrics_metrics.description: When including externally produced graphics, generate them at the correct final size instead of scaling them during inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scaling can change line widths, label sizes, and legibility; create graphics 'at the right size' to preserve intended proportions and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the same fonts in graphics and body text
rubrics_metrics.description: Fonts used in figures (labels, annotations) should match the document's main text fonts for visual consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency helps integrate graphics with the text; mismatched fonts across figures (from different programs) look unprofessional and distract readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match line widths between text and graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use line widths in graphics that harmonize with the stroke width of the document text (e.g., TEX typical stem ~0.4 pt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals require minimum line widths (e.g., ≥0.5 pt). Ensure line thicknesses in graphics are neither too thin nor too heavy compared to text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent color coding between text and graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the same color semantics in graphics as you do in the text (e.g., red for emphasis) while also respecting logical intrinsic color associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If red signals emphasis in text, use red for emphasis in graphics. Also consider conventional mappings (green=positive, red=alert). Do not choose colors arbitrarily; use colors to group and direct attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a single graphics program when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing figures with multiple tools often yields inconsistent fonts, line widths, and styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using one graphics tool (or a consistent toolchain) simplifies achieving uniform appearance across all figures and reduces integration problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label formatting consistency and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels in graphics should follow the same formatting and mathematical/units notation as the main text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent: if you write '1/2' in the text, do not use '0.5' in the graphic; use the same symbols (π not 3.141, e^{-iπ} not -1). Maintain consistent formatting across all labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labels must be legible
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure label size, contrast, and placement make them readable and not obscured by other elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tiny fonts, low-resolution rendering, or placing labels over lines or other text. Ensure labels remain legible at final reproduction size and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place labels next to the labeled object (avoid legend-only references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever space allows, place labels adjacent to the thing they describe to avoid forcing the reader to jump back and forth to a legend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary, draw a subdued leader line from label to object; avoid relying only on an external legend when immediate context is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdue unimportant labels to focus attention
rubrics_metrics.description: De-emphasize less important labels (e.g., using gray) so the reader's attention is drawn to the most relevant parts of the graphic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use low-contrast or lighter rendering for tertiary labels so they don't compete visually with primary data or annotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure a plot is justified: enough data points to merit plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether there are sufficient data points (or whether the reader needs a visual representation); if not, use a table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the dataset is small (a few numbers) or exact values are important, a table often conveys the information more effectively and with higher information density than a plot. Example: small-category feedback with few counts is better shown in a table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make plots convey data clearly (avoid obfuscating features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design plots so viewers can read values, discern comparisons, and get the intended message without confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary 3D, distracting background lines, ambiguous axis scales/units, rotated hard-to-read labels, or colors that have no grouping purpose. Bars/markers should not hide exact values—if exact numbers matter, show them or use a table. Avoid decorative effects that reduce information density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 3D pie charts and 3D effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-dimensional rendering of pies or bars distorts area/height perception and adds no useful information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 3D setups distort relative sizes (especially small slices), make comparisons harder, and are considered 'chart junk.' Use 2D charts or tables; do not add shading/3D purely for decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply colors or patterns randomly
rubrics_metrics.description: Color and pattern choices should direct focus or group related items, not serve as arbitrary decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid background patterns (crosshatch, diagonal lines) as substitutes for color—these distract. Avoid using color choices that contradict semantic expectations (e.g., making an insignificant category brightest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid background images, shadings, and clipart
rubrics_metrics.description: Background images, shadings, or clipart usually distract and seldom add important information to a graphic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep backgrounds unobtrusive (low contrast) or absent. Decorative elements that draw attention away from data should be removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize distracting graphical primitives (strong contrasts, dense grids, dashed lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove or tone down elements that immediately capture the eye but do not carry useful information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong contrasts draw attention first; grids and help lines should be low contrast and loosely spaced. Dashed/dotted lines create many high-contrast points and are generally poor for differentiating curves—use color instead. Background patterns are usually distracting and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use color rather than dashing to differentiate data series
rubrics_metrics.description: The eye groups by color more reliably than by dashing patterns; dashed lines can lose data points and be distracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer distinct colors (with attention to colorblind-safe palettes) to separate series. If color is not an option (e.g., print), use clear variations in line weight or markers rather than many dashed patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'chart junk'—eliminate non-informative decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove elements that do not convey data or help understanding; strive for high information density and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of chart junk: superfluous 3D, heavy background lines, gratuitous shading or patterns, unnecessary decorative imagery. If an element doesn't help the reader understand the data or message, remove it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steer attention intentionally; avoid unwanted distractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the page/graphic's goal is to avoid distractions (novel-like reading) or to steer attention (magazine/newspaper style) and design accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For main body text and dense reading, minimize distractions and use subtle emphasis (italics). For pages intended to guide scanning, use larger fonts, headlines, and layout to steer attention, but once the reader engages deeper, the main text and figures should revert to low-distraction typography.
